newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller to Russia amid missile worries.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller to Russia amid missile worries.

text.p: Turkey's Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller this week travels to Russia on a visit during which Ankara's concern Moscow may sell missiles to Cyprus threatens to overshadow talks on joint energy projects.

"The energy ministry is working on increasing the capacity of the existing natural gas line between the two countries and, given Turkey's growing natural gas needs, on building a new gas pipeline from Russia -- this will be on the agenda," a foreign ministry official told Reuters on Monday.
Ciller departs on Tuesday, fresh from talks with the European Union, which she blasted for unfairly shutting NATO-member Turkey out of its plans to admit new members.
A veiled warning by her that Ankara could block the planned expansion of NATO is likely to be welcomed in Moscow, which strongly opposes eastward extension of the organisation.

But media reports that Russia may sell surface-to-air S-300 missile systems to the Cyprus government may cloud the atmosphere. The Turkish foreign ministry said the matter of missile sales would be on the agenda.

"There are enough weapons on the island. The message will be given that instead of giving support to arming the Greek Cypriot side, they shoud convince them to sit at the (negotiating) table," a ministry official said.
Greek Cypriot officials say talks have been held with Russia on buying weapons, but refuse to say what kind.

The Mediterranean island is the site of a heavy military build-up and at the heart of tense relations between Turkey and Greece, which are also soured by territorial disputes in the Aegean Sea and minority rights.
Around 35,000 Turkish troops are stationed in northern Cyprus, which Turkey invaded in 1974 in the wake of a coup on the island engineered by the military then ruling in Athens.
The joint construction of a gas pipeline between Russia and Turkey is regarded by Turkey as essential to ward off energy shortages in the future, the ministry official said.

Turkey in September signed a memorandum of understanding for a $1.1 billion deal with Russia to build a 1,160-km (720-mile) pipeline with a capacity of up to 16 billion cubic metres of gas a year and to raise the capacity of the existing pipeline via the Balkans from eight billion cubic metres to 14 billion.
Similar accord on oil pipelines is unlikely as the two countries are involved in a tug-of-war over Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey opposes plans supported by Russia for a pipeline to transport oil from Azerbaijan to the Black Sea via Georgia or the Russian port of Novorossiisk.
